analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style health insurance program for all children and raises wages, child care, and housing help for low-income families.
analysis.headline: A children's omnibus bill with 109 House cosponsors, including 4 Republicans, was referred to six committees in May 2001, never received a vote in any committee or on the House floor, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill is a dozen anti-poverty and child-health bills rolled into one. It would automatically enroll every child born after 2002 in a new 'MediKids' health insurance program modeled on Medicare, let families of disabled children buy into Medicaid, give the FDA authority over tobacco marketing to kids, extend Brady background checks to gun shows, and require child gun locks. It also raises the minimum wage, expands the earned income tax credit, funds child care and Head Start, creates housing vouchers, and extends unpaid family leave to employers with 25 or more workers. It was referred to six House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 11 million uninsured children the bill's findings cite would get automatic health coverage. Families of disabled children earning up to three times the poverty line could buy Medicaid coverage. Low-wage workers would get a higher minimum wage and a bigger earned income tax credit. Low-income parents would get help with child care, Head Start, housing vouchers, and food stamps. Children in foster care, kids exposed to domestic violence, and juveniles in the justice system would get new services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children and low-wage working families

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after December 31, 2002 would be automatically enrolled at birth in a MediKids program covering Medicare-style core benefits, all required Medicaid children's benefits, and prescription drugs, with no cost-sharing for families below 150% of poverty [S3].

Families of disabled children with income up to 300% of poverty could purchase Medicaid coverage for their child, and states could expand Medicaid and SCHIP eligibility to 300% of poverty with sliding-scale premiums [S3].

The bill raises the minimum wage on a graduated schedule and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands, sets poverty-level wage standards for federal contract workers, and expands the earned income tax credit for larger families and married couples [S2].
It authorizes child care provider retention grants and scholarships, full-day full-year Head Start expansion, prekindergarten grants, school construction bonds, and federal child care centers [S2].
It creates a rental assistance voucher program, a National Affordable Housing Trust Fund, and low-income housing preservation grants [S2].

It gives the FDA authority over tobacco products with restrictions on marketing and youth access, requires Brady background checks at gun shows, mandates child handgun safety locks, and bans imports of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Families would pay MediKids premiums through their tax filings, with an exemption below 150% of poverty and a cap at 5% of adjusted gross income; the Treasury Secretary would be required to propose a schedule of progressive tax increases to fund the program as enrollment grows [S3]. Tobacco and firearms companies would bear the cost of new regulation and compliance. Employers with 25 to 49 employees would face new family-leave obligations, and federal contractors would have to pay a living wage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, tobacco firms, gun sellers, small employers

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a large new entitlement whose long-term financing is left open: it directs the Treasury Secretary to 'propose' a schedule of progressive tax increases within a year of enactment rather than specifying how the MediKids program will be funded in the out-years [S3].
Extending the Family and Medical Leave Act from employers with 50 employees down to 25 imposes unpaid-leave administration on thousands of small businesses [S2].
The MediKids premium applies broadly to families above the poverty exemption, a new household tax filing obligation layered on top of existing health coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: near-universal children's health coverage, a higher wage floor, child care, and housing help for low-income families. The honest cost is fiscal design: a major new entitlement funded partly by premiums on moderate-income families and partly by tax increases left to a later proposal, plus real compliance burdens on small employers. The scale is the kind of package that usually gets broken into separate bills; as a single omnibus it asked Congress to accept all of it or nothing, and it got neither.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees at once, then bounced among nine subcommittees, and no committee ever reported it back for a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California introduced the bill on May 24, 2001 with 25 original cosponsors, including Republicans Benjamin Gilman, Connie Morella, and Steven LaTourette [S3].

The presiding officer referred it not to one committee but to six at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Agriculture, Judiciary, and Financial Services — each for 'a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' [S5].

Over the next two months it was passed down to nine subcommittees across those committees, including Ways and Means Health and Human Resources, Energy and Commerce Health, and five Education and the Workforce subcommittees [S5].
Fifteen of the original cosponsors, including most of the bill's Republican and swing-district members, had their names deleted from the bill two days after introduction [S3].
The final cosponsor list stood at 109: 104 of 208 House Democrats, 4 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent [S4].
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No child gained coverage. The tobacco companies, insurers, and firearms dealers the bill would have regulated were spared new rules, employers avoided the expanded leave mandate and living wage requirement, and higher-income households never faced the MediKids premium or the progressive tax financing it would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco, gun, and insurance interests; not children

for.name: Rep. Bernie Sanders
for.role: House Independent, sole member of his party

against.role: Controls bill referral and floor scheduling

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Brady background checks to gun shows and new firearms mandates, a position it pressed throughout this period

sides.party_line_note: 104 of 208 House Democrats cosponsored, versus 4 of 223 House Republicans and the chamber's one Independent; 15 original bipartisan cosponsors dropped off two days after introduction, and no roll call ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill grants the FDA authority over tobacco products, restricting marketing, advertising, and youth access. That regulation exists to protect children, so the industry's interest runs against the public's.

Background checks at gun shows, mandatory child safety locks, a ban on importing large-capacity magazines, and regulation of Internet sales raise compliance costs and restrict sales. These rules target child safety.

MediKids would deliver coverage through health plans meeting Medicare+Choice requirements, potentially routing millions of children through private insurers, but the bill also imposes children's health accountability standards on employer plans and mandates childhood immunization coverage.
The Family and Medical Leave Act's coverage floor drops from 50 to 25 employees, adding unpaid-leave obligations to thousands of small businesses. Workers at those firms gain the leave right.
The bill requires federal contractors to pay at least a poverty-level wage. The cost lands on contractors; the benefit goes to their lowest-paid workers.

industries.industry: Child care providers and Head Start programs
industries.note: Provider retention grants, scholarships, facilities financing, and expanded full-day Head Start flow public money into the sector to raise wages and capacity for serving low-income children.
